title: Ai trading learning
author: NeedleworkerGood903
selftext:
to get started, I had my ai system read 100 stock trading books, top sellers, most recommended etc. 

it got about 200 strats, which i backtested against 10 years of data. 

NOT A SINGLE STRAT WORKS LOL

which really shouldn't be a surprise. but it is really funny. 

i wonder if something went wrong, but if any of those worked everyone would be using it.

comments.author: Yellowlizardtv
comments.body:
Got a repo for this? Maybe a collection of markdowns for what the LLMs got from those books?
I figure there has to be some good repositories out there   like that, where it could save the rest of us from running essentially the same thing for the same info in general.

As for strategies, you'd have to modify them of course. The key is that you have a strong base now for your model to reference a lot of content for your future strategies. Similar to how references are important when developing other software with LLMs.

replies.author: wkerstens
replies.body: The thing is, once its public knowledge the edge disappears very quickly. This is easily testable on all papers explaining a researched strategy, it works in the years before the paper was released, and loses the edge quickly after.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: That result is common, and a clean "nothing works" is better than a fake winner. Before you trust it, I'd check that the backtests had the right rules, like using only past data at each step and including fees, since a bug can kill a good idea as easily as it can create a fake one. Many book strategies are described loosely, so the code might not match the author's intent. It's also worth testing for what the test could detect, by running it on a rule you know should work or on random data. Cymetica's Backtest Labs has a fee setting and a held out stretch of data for checks like that.
